facts.fact: Coore & Crenshaw, opened 2012; 13 par 3s; net proceeds go to the Wild Rivers Coast Alliance.
Part of the course's funding was to support conservation of the silvery phacelia, a flower threatened in Oregon that thrives at the resort.
Silvery phacelia has silvery, hairy leaves and white flower clusters.

current.subject: A western snowy plover on the sand (course chat, developer's call).
current.keep: The plover: a protected shorebird for a course that funds conservation.
current.weaknesses: Small and thin-legged at 1x; the sand base is a separate strip.

concepts.name: The Snowy Plover
concepts.rationale: A rounder, bigger plover with its real field marks: pale back, dark forehead bar, ear patch and breast patches, standing where the wave runs out.
concepts.symbolism: Small, protected, at home on the dunes, like the course's purpose.
concepts.strengths: Cute and clear; the field marks make it a real species.
concepts.tradeoffs: Another bird in a resort with many coastal animals.

concepts.name: Silvery Phacelia
concepts.rationale: The flower the Preserve was built to help: a coil of white flowers above silver leaves, on a dusk-green medallion.
concepts.symbolism: The name's real meaning: this course preserves something.
concepts.typography: Cormorant Garamond Italic for a botanical-plate feel.
concepts.strengths: Authentic and unexpected; nobody else owns it.
concepts.tradeoffs: A small white flower is subtle; few golfers know the plant.

recommendation: Concept 2. It carries the course's reason for existing, and the dark medallion makes it read at 1x.
